new_statements.quote: Halme 2004 (snippet): "... homonymous on tonal level. Baucom (1974) states that all Wambo languages employ two “tone phonemes”. He makes two interesting observations about ..." [Kwambi is in the same chapter's list: "Evale, Mbalanhu, Dombondola, Mbandja, Ndonga, Kwambi, Ngandjera, Kwaluudhi, Kolonkadhi and Eunda"]. Magnusson [2008] p.17: "6. TONE: The tonology of the Bantu languages is generally a highly complex issue. According to Baucom (1972:53) differences in tone are often mentioned by Wambo speakers as the main differences between the dialects. In my view, the topic of tone would be best treated by a native speaker with linguistic training, a task that is still waiting for its man (or woman)."
new_statements.citation: Second-hand: Halme, Riikka. 2004. A Tonal Grammar of Kwanyama. Köln: Köppe (reporting Baucom 1974 [=1972/1975]); supporting first-hand context: Magnusson, Lars. [2008]. The Wambo dialect Kwambi as compared to Ndonga. Unpublished ms, UNAM, section 6 'Tone', p.17.
new_statements.locator: Halme 2004: archive.org full-text-search snippet of item tonalgrammarofkw00riik (introductory chapter on Wambo languages; page not recoverable from snippet); Magnusson [2008]: section 6 TONE, PDF p.17
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators. (1) (32 pp., PDF created 2008-06-15, author 'Lars'): extracted text of page 17 gives exactly "6. TONE: The tonology of the Bantu languages is generally a highly complex issue. According to Baucom (1972:53) differences in tone are often mentioned by Wambo speakers as the main differences between the dialects. In my view, the topic of tone would be best treated by a native speaker with linguistic training, a task that is still waiting for its man (or woman)." I read the surrounding sections: section 4 (sound correspondences) is purely segmental (liquid tap vs lateral, affricate ch, class-prefix vowels, vowel length in the cl.4/…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kwambi, like all Wambo (R.20) varieties, is reported (second-hand, via Halme citing Baucom) to have a two-tone (H/L) system; no source opened says anything about the position of word stress or accent in Kwambi. The only open primary description (Magnusson) treats segments and morphology and explicitly leaves tone undescribed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Homburger 1949's generic 'In Bantu the dynamic accent is on the penultimate syllable in the southern...' is not tied to Kwambi and was seen only as a snippet.)
new_statements.domain_note: No word- vs phrase-level prominence statement exists in the opened material; the tone report is a family-level generalisation over all Wambo languages, not a Kwambi-specific analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: All material concerns Kwambi proper (Oshikwambi/Otshikwambi/'Ochikwambi', Uukwambi district, central Owambo; Glottolog kwam1251, ISO kwm, Guthrie R.23). Magnusson's corpus is mostly eastern and central Uukwambi (Okatana, Elim); he notes possible tonal differences east vs west and nasal-drop in the far-western Onaanda area. The tone statement found is a generalisation over all Wambo/R.20 varieties (Baucom via Halme), not Kwambi-specific.

sources.citation: Magnusson, Lars. [2008; cited on Wikipedia as 2003]. The Wambo dialect Kwambi as compared to Ndonga. Unpublished manuscript, University of Namibia. 32 pp. (PDF created 2008-06-15; retrieved from Wayback capture of lars.eyra.se/)
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent anywhere (grepped stress|accent|penult|prosod|pitch: 0 hits). Section 4 'Sound correspondences' is segmental only; section 6 'TONE' (PDF p.17) is five lines that decline to treat tone: 'According to Baucom (1972:53) differences in tone are often mentioned by Wambo speakers as the main differences between the dialects. In my view, the topic of tone would be best treated by a native speaker with linguistic training...'; section 9 repeats 'the present study is not concerned with the tonology of the dialect'.

sources.citation: Fivaz, Derek. 1986. A Reference Grammar of Oshindonga (Ndonga). Windhoek: The Academy, Department of African Languages, University of Namibia. [2nd rev. ed. 2003, with Sakaria Shikomba]
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Magnusson's Kwambi description is explicitly differential against Ndonga ('features which are not mentioned as being different are as described for the grammar... of the closest literary dialect') and reports no prosodic difference; Fivaz's Ndonga grammar has a tone/length chapter and is the de facto statement of accent/penultimate behaviour that Kwambi would inherit by that method. Proxy only (Ndonga R.22, not Kwambi), hence low priority.
